paper.title: A portable high-quality random number generator for lattice field theory simulations (RANLUX)
paper.venue: Computer Physics Communications 79, 100 (1994); builds on Marsaglia and Zaman, Annals of Applied Probability 1(3), 1991

program.how: written for ounce-core from the subtract-with-carry recurrence and the block-decimation rule as specified in the C++ standard's engine definitions (the parameters and seeding procedure were taken from the standard's text); no third-party code copied
program.target: static freestanding aarch64 Linux ELF, run with `ounce-core run-elf`

claims_checked: ranlux24 (ranlux24_base keeping 23 of every 223 values), 10000th output 9901578
ranlux48 (ranlux48_base keeping 11 of every 389 values), 10000th output 249142670248501

expected_values_source.what: the 10000th-invocation values required by the C++ standard draft ([rand.predef]) for ranlux24_base, ranlux48_base, ranlux24 and ranlux48; the engine and seeding definitions are from the same document ([rand.eng.sub], [rand.adapt.disc])
expected_values_source.note: the values are data, copied as numbers. They are published by the C++ standard, which defines these engines after Marsaglia-Zaman and Luscher; they are NOT numbers printed in Luscher's 1994 paper or in his own ranlux distribution (that tarball was not fetched). The author's page confirms the paper reference and that the C++ library contains the generator. Only the luxury parameters the standard fixes (p=223 and p=389) are run

negative_control: built with -DRANLUX_S24=11 (short lag 11 instead of 10 for the 24-bit generators), ranlux24_base prints 6dc569 instead of 791fa0 and ranlux24 prints 964018 instead of 97160a (two FAIL), the 48-bit generators still pass, and the program exits 1 (checked on ounce-core Tier-3 and natively)
not_checked: the chaos / Lyapunov-exponent analysis and the statistical claims of the paper (that decimation removes the correlations of plain subtract-with-carry)
the other luxury levels of Luscher's ranlux (0 to 4, p = 24, 48, 97, 223, 389) and the single/double-precision float versions of his C implementation
exactly the 10000th value only: no longer output sequence is compared
speed figures (emulator run time says nothing about the authors' hardware)
Tier-4 and native ARM64 execution (the native comparison is x86-64)
what_a_pass_means: this program, run on ounce-core, produces the four values the C++ standard requires for the RANLUX-derived engines. It does not show the statistical claims hold.
